title: What the state spends to speak well of itself
intro: Official advertising is tax money. It comes out of the same account that pays for nurseries, ambulances and sewage networks — and the bill is bigger than the figure the government publishes, because since 2017 the state-owned companies dropped out of the system where that spending was reported.
rulers.broad.label: Broad ruler: government plus the main state-owned companies
rulers.broad.explain: Campaigns by the ministries, by the government communications office and by the state-owned companies — Banco do Brasil, Caixa, BNDES and others. Figures adjusted for inflation to December 2024.
rulers.broad.rows[1].note: R$ 7.1 billion over the full term
rulers.broad.finding: Lula 3 spends 15% more per year than Bolsonaro on the same basis. Over the first two years of each government the gap is wider: 31% above what Bolsonaro spent in 2019 and 2020. In two years, the current government has already used 58% of everything the previous one spent in four.
rulers.narrow.label: Narrow ruler: the advertising budget alone
rulers.narrow.explain: The budget allocated to official advertising, without the state-owned companies. It is the ruler most headlines use — and the smaller of the two.
rulers.narrow.years[0].note: the lowest in ten years — the peak year of the pandemic
question: R$ 2 billion a year for the state to speak well of itself. It is tax money, out of the same account — and the part you can check is only the smaller half. How much of it did you see turn into something built?
transparency.title: The blackout cost R$ 1.4 million a year to happen
transparency.costLabel: was the annual cost of the institute that collected and published federal advertising data
transparency.watchedLabel: is what is spent on official advertising each year, government and state-owned companies combined
transparency.timeline[0].what: The institute collected and organised federal advertising data. Any citizen could request detailed campaign-by-campaign figures under the freedom of information act.
transparency.timeline[1].what: The advertising agencies, which funded the institute with a percentage of what they billed on government contracts, stopped paying. The institute closed.
transparency.timeline[2].what: The government did not step in — it neither took on the cost nor created a replacement. The state-owned companies dropped out of the system.
transparency.timeline[3].what: Petrobras, Caixa, Banco do Brasil, Correios and BNDES report on their own, with little detail and outside the government system. Two governments have passed since then, from opposite sides, and neither rebuilt the institute.
transparency.punch: Keeping the watchdog cost 0.07% of what it watched. Nobody picked up the bill.
